pt1_01.en: A generational chart spanning the 2nd through 10th generations (世), giving the personal names (mostly ordinal 'nth-lang' names such as Nianer-lang 念二郎, Yi-lang 一郎, Qian-yi-lang 千一郎) and some spouses (e.g. wife of the Luo 羅, Zeng 曾, and other clans). Dated at the top to the Wanli wuchen year (Wanli 44, 1616). A header note records that descendants of various lords (e.g. Wentong 文通, Tongfu 通福, Hua 化, and the brothers Nianyi-lang through Nianwu-lang) settled in different places: Fuzhou prefecture (福州府), Guangdong province, Dapu (大埔), Bulan (埔藍), and Chengxiang (程鄉). Names and places are partly [unclear] and a few entries are illegible.

pt1_02.en: A long generational register covering roughly the 15th through 23rd generations (世) — including the 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st, 22nd and 23rd generations. It lists personal names by generation (e.g. Chao- 朝, Ri- 日, Yuan- 元, Tong- 通, Shao- 紹, Cheng- 承, Da- 大, Yong- 永, Jun- 俊 naming series) together with notes on which descendants lived where (e.g. settlements at Yongxi 永溪, Yongning-bao 永寧堡, Yong'an-bao 永安堡, Longshan-xiang 龍山巷, Dongshan 東山, Donghu 東湖, etc.). Many entries are marked 嗣詳 / 嗣未詳 ('lineage [un]recorded'). Several characters and place names are [unclear] (illegible).

pt1_03.en: A generational register covering roughly the 9th through 12th generations (世), listing personal names in naming series — the Chao- 超 series (9th gen), the Tong- 通 / Shao- 紹 series, the Cheng- 承 series (10th gen), Daxin 大信 (11th gen), and the 12th generation (Yongzong 永宗 styled Mindao 敏道, Yongren 永仁 styled Rentang 任堂, Yonghong 永宏 styled Shaohan 韶涵), plus a closing line of Jun- 俊 names. The header characters (天世/大世/二世/三世) are partly [unclear].

pt1_04.en: An origin essay on the Jiang (江) surname's descent and migrations. It opens with the principle that one must trace lineage to its source — as mountains spring from the Kunlun (崑崙) range and rivers from the essence of heaven, so people must trace back to their founding ancestor. The Jiang clan descends from the line of Bo Yi (伯益), enfeoffed at Jingyang (涇陽); the family took the place name Jiang as its surname. Later they lived at Jiyang (濟陽), which gave rise to the alternate clan-seat name 'Jiyang commandery.' Jingyang lies not far from the Huai (淮) and Xiang (湘) rivers — this was the starting point of the line's origin in Shandong. The line later passed to Jiangxi, to Raozhou (饒州), over more than fifty generations, down to the descendants of 'Sangu' (三古) and 'Wuzhai' (五齋). 'Sangu' refers to Wanli (萬里) and his two brothers, three men in all [the exact relationships here are somewhat [unclear] in the original]; 'Wuzhai' is named after one held in the tradition. Afterward they moved to Henan (豫) province and the Fujian–Guangdong (閩粵) region — all are this clan's offshoots.

pt1_05.en: A set of ancestral-hall couplets (對聯) with brief framing prose. It notes that the genealogy is fragmentary and incomplete, so firm proof is lacking, yet from what can be seen and heard one can still trace where the ancestors came from. It then records couplets for ancestral halls: a couplet for the provincial-city ancestral hall ('The line descends from Sangu 三古; sacrifices are offered at Wuyang 五羊 / Wuxun 五羊…'), evoking the ancestors' virtue and merit deserving lasting commemoration; and a couplet for the Yongding (永定) ancestral hall, praising the clan's flourishing and its branching into legitimate descent lines. Further lines celebrate learned and worthy men of the family and the virtues of loyalty and filial piety in serving family and state. The piece is signed with respectful authorship by a clansman holding the 'fubang' (副榜, secondary-list) examination rank. Some phrasing is literary and a few readings are [unclear].

pt1_06.en: A page of ancestral-hall couplets / commemorative verse, written in vertical columns. The lines praise literary and official attainment (alluding to Han-dynasty learning, broad mastery of the Classics, brilliant 'five-flower' literary talent reaching far) and the family virtues of loyalty and filial piety in serving the state, alongside references to the ancestor Bo Yi (伯益) and the clan's noble descent. Side columns again carry the respectful signature of a descendant holding the 'fubang' (副榜, secondary-list) rank. Because the text is laid out as fragmented vertical couplet-columns, the continuous sense is hard to reconstruct and several readings are [unclear]; this is a faithful-but-tentative rendering of the couplets' gist rather than a line-by-line translation.

pt1_07.en: A textual-research note on the Jiang (江) surname, citing the comprehensive history 'Gangjian Daquan' (綱鑑大全). It traces the descent: a descendant of Zhuanxu [鬚/顓頊, here written 顯頃, likely a copyist variant] named Nü Xiu (女修) bore Da Ye (大業); Da Ye's wife Nü Hua (女莘) bore Gao [Yao]. This is Lord Bo Yi (伯益), who aided Yu the Great (禹) in controlling the floods; for his merit the sage-king Shun granted him the surname Ying (嬴), and Yu recommended him to Heaven. His eldest son was Da Lian (大廉), whose descendants became the states of Qin (秦) and Zhao (趙). It then quotes the 'Basic Annals' of Sima Qian (司馬遷): the ancestors of Qin were of the Ying surname, and their descendants, enfeoffed with states, took those states as surnames — yielding the Xu (徐), Zheng (鄭/郯), Ge (葛), Zhongli (終黎), Yan (奄) and other clans, including the Liang (梁), Huang (黃) and Jiang (江) surnames. The closing source citation ('from the Shiji 史記') and one character are [unclear].

pt1_08.en: The opening of a Jiang clan preface (江氏族序), with a heading naming Liujiu-lang (六九郎) and the noble-titled Qigong (貴七公), and the senior wife née Yan (顏氏, 'Daniang'), and a signed attribution to a respectful compiler of Xin'an (新安孝肅謹誌). The preface reflects that people, like water and trees, all have a source and a root, and like bamboo and pine all strive to bud and flourish; descendants who lose touch with their root cannot honor their distant ancestors nor secure their posterity. Thus all of one branch belong to the ancestors' unified line, and over countless generations the hope rests on later descendants carrying it forward. It alludes to the auspicious omens of the 'five cassia' (五桂) and 'three locust-trees' (三槐) foretelling high office, and exhorts the clan to strive. Tracing the clan's origin to high antiquity, it again identifies the founder as descended from Lord Bo Yi (伯益), enfeoffed at Jiang (江) and taking the state as the surname — continuing onto the next page.

pt1_09.en: A continuation of the clan preface, surveying notable forebears once the surname and dwelling-places became recorded from the Qin and Han onward. It alludes to Jiang ancestors celebrated in the histories: one 'Lord Gan' (澉公) who, in a dream of plucking blossoms, displayed literary refinement in the Southern Dynasties; another who carved verse and won fame for talent in the 'Nan Shi' (南史, History of the Southern Dynasties); references to filial and benevolent conduct; to Jiang Gan's village (江澉鄉) and to figures of Song times who declined office or were honored for loyalty and chastity to the Zhao (趙, Song) house, and to fame passed down through two men's sons. The passage is densely allusive and fragmentary, several names and a whole illegible segment are [unclear], so this is a tentative reading of its drift rather than a precise rendering.

pt1_10.en: A migration narrative tracing the clan's descent and movements. It recounts honoring the teachings of ancestor Chongxun-gong (重訓公) across distant generations, and carefully verifying the lineage's branches. The clan's line is said to issue from the left bank of the Yellow River (河左 / Hezuo), branching at Huaiyang (淮陽), and originally residing in Fujian — at Zhangzhou prefecture (漳州府), Lihua [Lyding] county [漳/利定縣, [unclear] reading], Zhangnan-li (漳南里), beneath the osmanthus tree at Wulongping (烏垅坪). Passing through the Song–Yuan–Ming transition, the great senior line of earlier generations was scattered and lost. Then in the 3rd year of Longqing of the Ming (隆慶三年, 1569), the founding ancestor Zichuan-gong (紫川公) together with his uncle Huailong-gong (懷龍公) moved to Yong'an county (永安縣), Huizhou prefecture (惠州府), Guangdong — to the Xiayi-yue (下義約) district, settling at Shanzixia (山子下) and Maju (馬聚), where two lines lived together as a clan. The land was auspicious and prospered its people, uniting the surname among worthy neighbors under the blessings of their forebears — continuing onto the next page.

pt1_11.en: The conclusion of the clan preface / migration narrative. It mentions the wife of Renmu (仁穆) and her three sons who settled at Gaoluo (高羅), and lists a group of 'Chao-' named uncles and granduncles (Chaoying 潮纓, Chaohuo 潮活, Chaochun 潮淳, Chaojun 潮浚, Chaohao 潮浩, Chaoxi 潮錫, Chaozong 潮宗, Chaoyang 潮陽). As the people grew numerous they again moved to a new district; the eight or nine brothers scattered to different places, branching into perhaps a hundred households yet numbering several thousand of one ancestral stock — some entering the official schools, some among the common people, some holding office. The text exhorts descendants to remember the trunk-and-root, water-and-source bond, to repay their origins, to honor the ancestors, and to keep the whole surname united in one hall so that blessings extend for a hundred generations and the line flourishes for ten thousand years. It closes 'thus is this preface' (是為序), followed by the start of an examination-honors note recording a Ming Jiajing dingwei-year (Jiajing 26, 1547) presented scholar (進士).

pt1_12.en: A near-duplicate variant of the preface's closing passage (cf. page 11), exhorting worthy descendants to remember the family heritage, carry on the family's good name through the generations, repay their origins, honor the ancestors, and keep the kinsmen harmonious in one hall — so that blessings extend for a hundred generations and the line flourishes endlessly (the 'guadie' 瓜瓞 trailing-gourd image of unbroken posterity), closing 'thus is this preface' (是為序). It is followed by a heading 'Examination honors through the generations' (歷代科甲題名) and one entry: Jiang Wanren (江萬仞), presented scholar (進士) of the Ming Jiajing dingwei year (Jiajing 26, 1547), who served as Court Vicar [寺卿] of Wu county (吳縣), registered at Jinjiang (晉江).

pt1_13.en: A register of examination degree-holders (科甲題名) of the Jiang clan, mostly from the Kangxi and Qianlong reigns. Each line gives a name, the degree and examination year, often an official post, and the place of registration (籍) — e.g. Jiang Zhongshi (江中柿), presented scholar (進士) of the Ming Wanli bingchen year (Wanli 44, 1616) [post partly [unclear]]; Jiang Heqing (江河清), provincial graduate (舉人) of Kangxi wuzi (1708), registered at Shanghang (上杭); Jiang Lianhui (江聯輝), juren of Kangxi guisi (1713); Jiang Xunlong (江循龍), military juren of Kangxi gengxu (1670); plus several Qianlong-era juren and military juren (e.g. Jiang Longchi 江龍池, Jiang Fengqing 江風清, Jiang Huan 江煥, Jiang Qianda 江乾達, Jiang Yuanchuan 江元川, Jiang Fengming 江鳳鳴). Many served as county instructors (教諭). Registrations span Yongding (永定), Shanghang (上杭), Houguan (侯官) and other places; one year-character is [unclear].

pt1_14.en: A register of Qianlong-era examination degree-holders of the Jiang clan, largely overlapping with the previous page (a variant listing). Entries include Jiang Longchi (江龍池), juren of Qianlong bingchen (1736), registered at Yongding; Jiang Fengqing (江風清), juren of Qianlong bingchen (1736), county instructor of Houguan; Jiang Huan (江煥), juren of Qianlong renwu (1762), instructor of Guangze (光澤) county; Jiang Qianda (江乾達), juren of Qianlong wuzi (1768), magistrate of Xintai (新泰), Shandong, registered at Hangzhou; Jiang Yuanchuan (江元川), juren of Qianlong dingyou (1777), instructor at Lehe/Lehui (樂合/樂會), Guangdong; Jiang Fengming (江鳳鳴), juren of Qianlong wuzi (1768), Hanlin Academy; and Jiang Lilong (江麗龍), military juren of Qianlong wuzi (1768). Some place names and one or two characters differ slightly from page 13 and are [unclear].

pt1_15.en: A register of further Qianlong-era (and one earlier-reign) examination degree-holders of the Jiang clan. Entries include Jiang Youlong (江游龍), military xiucai/graduate of Qianlong guihai (1743), serving as a regional commander (都司); Jiang Guilan (江桂蘭), preferential tribute student (優貢) of Qianlong yimao and juren of the gengshen year; Jiang Shichun (江世春), tribute student (拔貢) of Qianlong xinyou, magistrate of Dongshan (東山), Sichuan, registered at Yongding; Jiang Hao (江浩), tribute student of Qianlong dingyou, professor (教授) of Zhangzhou prefecture, registered at Shanghang; Jiang Yicheng (江以成), of Qianlong bingwu; Jiang Daozhuang (江道莊), military juren of Jiaqing jiazi (1804); Jiang Chengrui (江呈瑞), juren of Qianlong xinmao; and Jiang Shaoyan (江紹淹), stipend student (廩生) [reign-name 永熙 is likely a copyist error and is [unclear]], registered at Changle (長樂).

pt1_16.en: A biographical ancestral-record entry for the 2nd-generation ancestor Shi'er-lang (二世祖十二郎), courtesy name Wanshuo (萬碩), styled Guwu (古屋), buried together with his wife née Qian ('Jiuniang' 錢氏九娘) at Sanbu-xiang, Gongkang (工杭三埠鄉). It records his Song-dynasty learning (明經) and offices — academician/instructor, Hanlin Academy secretary (中書), Vice Minister of the Left in the Ministry of Revenue (戶部左侍郎), prefect of Nanjian-zhou (南劍州), and a military commander rank — noting that he and his two brothers all rendered great merit. It then traces descendants: his son Songgong (宋公) fled warfare into Fujian (閩) and lived in seclusion at Yangban-li (陽板里); the eldest son (courtesy name Guokai 國凱, styled Xiangzhai 祥齋) and a second son settled at Yangban-li; a grandson Zhuoxin (濯新) bore five sons, the eldest Mengde (孟德) moving to Xiandong-hengkeng, Haiyang county (海陽縣), Chaozhou. Later branches settled at Zhao'an (詔安), Xinghua (興化), and other places; it also notes an alternate account in a separate Fuqing (福慶) genealogy that Wanshuo-gong had five sons. Several characters are [unclear].

pt1_17.en: Founding ancestor Jiang Baliang (江公八郎), styled Wenming (文明). His wife was Lady Zhang Yiniang (張一娘); the couple was buried together at Fuqing Garden, Erping Village (福慶苑二坪邨). According to the record, Lord Baliang moved here from Shibi in Ninghua (寧化石壁) to Shanghang (上杭), and at Sanping, Deng (三坪鄧) established the family's foundation and livelihood. He produced three main branches: the eldest, Lord Wanli (萬里); the second, Lord Wanzai (萬載); the third, Lord Wanqing (萬頃). His wife, of the Bai (白) clan, was honored as a first-rank lady. The elder ancestor Lord Wanli, posthumously titled Wenzhong (文忠), named Lin (臨), styled Guxin (古心), passed the Song-dynasty Chunyou (淳祐) presented-scholar (jinshi) examination, was a top graduate (zhuangyuan) under Emperor Duanzong, rose through office to Minister (Shangshu), and was appointed Commander of the Embroidered-Uniform Guard (Jinyiwei) and also to the Ministry of Rites. He had three sons: the eldest Wanwen (萬文), the second Wanqi (萬錡), the third Wanjian (萬鑑); his wife was of the Zhang (張) clan. The elder ancestor Lord Wanzai, posthumously titled Marquis Wusu (武肅侯), named Yi (億), styled Gushan (古山), was appointed Commander of the Embroidered-Uniform Guard and also to the Ministry of Rites. He had two sons: the eldest Lun (侖), the second Niu (鈕). [Note: the Song-era ranks and offices attributed here are as written in the genealogy and are not independently verified.]

pt1_18.en: A spouse-and-descendant register for the early generations descending from Baliang (八郎): his wife of the Que (闕) clan, then Nian'erlang (念二郎) and his wife of the Lei (雷) clan, their three sons, and the line through Guanxin (灌新公), with wives' surnames (Xiao, Chen, Wu, etc.), numbers of sons, and personal names. It also records the grave of Lady Chen Liuniang (陳六娘) at Guihuashu-xia, Wuyi, in Yongding County (永定縣武藝桂花樹下), described with fengshui terms (a 'horseshoe-crab swimming the lake' formation). The text itself notes uncertainty about how many sons each mother bore ('数量有待參考', numbers remain to be verified).

pt1_19.en: Covers the 2nd-generation ancestor Baliang and the uncle-ancestors Nian'sanlang, Nian'yilang, and Nian'wulang, with their wives and sons, opening with a couplet praising the locale ('green hills as a screen, five sons born, the line spreading through Fujian and Guangdong, examination successes rising'). It records the dispersal of the five sons into five great branches — the eldest settling at Shangtao, others moving to Dabu Fengping (大埔豐坪), Pulan Shumi (埔藍樹密), and Chengxiang Zhegu-keng (程鄉鷓鴣坑) — and gives burial sites in Yong'an, Tingzhou Prefecture, Fujian (福建汀州府永安). Includes ancestors Bai'balang (百八郎) and Siliulang (四六郎).

pt1_20.en: A short register (overlapping with page 19) recording the five-branch dispersal — sons moving to Dabu Fengping, Pulan, and Chengxiang Zhegu-keng — and listing ancestors Bai'balang (百八郎, wife Lady Zhou Miaolian) with son Chuliu-gong (廚六公), Siliulang (四六郎), and the lineage ancestor Bai'sanlang (百三郎, wife Lady Xu Miaoxiang) with two sons: Yijiulang named Guiqi (刈九郎諱貴七) and Liu'sanlang named Guiliu (六三郎諱貴六), with burial place at Aonan-li, Yongding County (永定縣澳南里).

pt1_21.en: Covers roughly the 5th generation. Records uncle-ancestor Liu'sanlang (named Guiliu), whose descendants flourished at Jinjiang, Quanzhou (泉州晉江); and the 5th-generation ancestor Liu'jiulang named Guiqi (六九郎諱貴七), with wife of the Lai (賴) clan and grave at Wushe-keng, Hannan-li, Yong'an County, Tingzhou Prefecture, Fujian. It notes a genealogical reconciliation: under the old An'xin (新安) genealogy Guiqi was treated as founding ancestor, but a joint genealogy compiled in 'Tongguang year 5' (通光五年 — likely a miswriting; possibly Daoguang/Tongzhi era, [unclear]) recovered four earlier generations, making Yilang named Wentong (文通) and Jiang Zi'erlang named Qitong (祺通) the true 5th-generation ancestors. Also lists Jiang Zi'erlang (祺通), buried at Hannan-li, Yongding, with two sons (the eldest Chengshan moving to Fuzhou).

pt1_22.en: Covers the 6th and 7th generations. Records the 6th-generation ancestor Jiang Zi'erlang named Wentong (文通公), wife of the Ma (馬) clan, with burial sites in Yongding County (永定縣汪坑 / 武藝坪) and two sons (eldest Dongshan 東山; second's name unrecorded). Includes notes reconciling a wife's surname (Wang 王 vs. another reading) across genealogies and a branch of six households settling at Changle County (長樂縣), plus the 7th-generation ancestor Dongshan-gong, wife of the Wu (巫) clan, with son Wenning Silang (文寧四郎). Several details are flagged in the original as uncertain.

pt1_23.en: A direct-line register from the 8th through 11th generations: 8th-gen ancestor Silang named Aiyu (四郎諱愛宇公, wife Lady Huang); 9th-gen Liulang (六郎公, wife Lady Shun) with son Zhiqing; 10th-gen Zhiqing-gong (志清公, wife Lady Wu) with son Dufu; and 11th-gen Dufu-gong (讀富公, wife Lady Zheng) with four sons — Yuanshan (元珊), Yuanyu (元玉), Yuanzhen (元珍), Yuanzhu (元珠). Includes burial locations in Yong'an with fengshui descriptions and grave-orientation notes.

pt1_24.en: An explanatory note plus register concerning the four 11th-generation brothers (sons of Dufu/Laifu) and their forebears Yili-gong (以立) and Yixian-gong (以賢) in Fujian, several of whose remains were cremated. It reconciles competing genealogies — one (the Li'an 利安 clan record) says Laifu-gong (賴富公) had four branches, not three — and notes that descendants of Yuanshan and Yuanzhu mostly settled at Zengcheng (增城), with knowledge confirmed through joint ancestral-hall gatherings in Guangdong. Lists elder-ancestor Yuanshan (元珊) and uncle-ancestor Yuanzhen (元珍) with their wives and a joint burial site at Shanzi-xia, Shali-jing (山子下沙瀝逕).

pt1_25.en: Continues the 11th/12th-generation lines. Records descendants of the Yuan-generation brothers: Huaiyun-gong styled Yiyu (懷韻公字以玉), whose descendants went to Yong'an Xiahua-yue, Shanzi-xia (永安下劃約山子下) to build an ancestral hall; Huaiyun's wife Lady Lin and four sons Daoquan, Daoxian, Daoying, Daoping (道全/道顯/道影/道屏); a note that Daoquan-gong (nicknamed 'Tiger-gong') lived plainly, prospered, and lived long (the figure given for his age, '八千', is clearly a copyist error — [unclear]). Also lists uncle-ancestor Yuanjue (元玨) and the lineage ancestor Yuanzhu (元珠, wife Lady Zeng), with a grave at Dabu and a Jiaqing-era (嘉慶) repair note.

pt1_26.en: Mostly grave/repair notes plus a short register. It describes a stone tablet and a Daoguang-era (道光) tomb renovation — work begun in a yi-hai year (乙亥, i.e. Daoguang 19 / 1839, [unclear]) — with grave-orientation details, and records that the ancestor produced four sons: Jichuan (繼川), Huaichuan (懷川), Rongchuan (榮川), Huachuan (華川). A note explains that the names carved inside the tomb differed from those used outside (Chongzu/Rongzu, Rongshu, Rongchuan, Ronghua), clarifying that 'Jichuan' is the same person as 'Rongzu-gong'.

pt1_27.en: Continues the four-brother (12th-13th generation) lines, equating outside-names with tomb-names: Huaichuan = Rongfu-gong, Huachuan = Rongrongwen. Records elder-ancestor Jichuan styled Rongzu (繼川公字榮祖, wife Lady Liu); Huaichuan styled Rongxiang (懷川公字榮祥), who moved to Guangzi Dongkeng (廣子東坑); uncle-ancestor Huachuan styled Ronghua (華川公字榮華, wife Lady Zhou) with two sons Daojun and Daoming and their descendants; and the 13th-generation ancestor Rongchuan styled Yixian (榮川公字以賢), with a Daoguang 3 (道光三年 = 1823) burial/repair note at Yong'an.

pt1_28.en: Mostly a grave-repair narrative for the 13th-generation ancestor's tomb. It records a renovation in a Daoguang yi-wei year (道光乙未 = Daoguang 15 / 1835), the adding-in of an ancestress of the Chen (陳) clan, and the discovery of old bones in the grass near the ancestral grave during the works — which were reburied nearby with a brick marker. It then gives the register: two main branches, the elder Daotong-gong (道通公) and the younger Daozhou-gong (道周公); uncle-ancestor Daozhou with son Wanlong (萬龍).

pt1_29.en: Covers the 14th generation and its sons. Records the 14th-generation ancestor Tong-gong (通公) and ancestress Lady Zhang, jointly buried at Xin'an Temple, Jinkeng (新安寺/金坑), with a grave-orientation note for a wu-chen year (戊辰). It lists the nine main branches (sons named Riyan, Riliang, Rihui, Riyao, Richan, Rican, Ribiao, Rikai, Rirun 日烟/日亮/日輝/日燿/日蟬/日燦/日標/日開/日閏), and one son's four grandsons Chaoyuan, Chaohai, Chaohao, Chaohu (潮源/潮海/潮浩/潮湖).

pt1_30.en: Covers the line of Chaoyuan-gong (潮源公) and related kin, with a notable migration: during the Kangxi era (康熙年間, late 17th–early 18th c.) Chaoyuan moved to Guangzhou Prefecture (廣州府), drew an official salary, and was promoted to qianzong (千總, a military rank); his wife Lady Liu bore sons who settled behind Buzhengsi Back Street in Guangzhou. It also records Chaodong-gong (潮東公, wife Lady Chen) and son Wenhe (文和), and Wenhe's three branches — Shihe, Shijin, Shihong (世和/世錦/世宏) — with their sons (the Jianxian, Jianhai, Jiangui, Jianmei generation), located at Yong'an.

pt1_31.en: Continues the Yong'an branches from page 30 (Shihe/Shijin/Shihong lines): Jianhai-gong with son A-yi; Shijin-gong's two sons Jingchang and Jianqing; Jianchang's three sons Qingxiu, Yongxiu, Weixiu; Shihong's one son Liexiu — all recorded as residing at Yong'an at the place named Yitian (亭田). It then lists the 3rd elder-ancestor Riwen-gong (日炆公, wife Lady Liu, three daughters, descendants unclear), the 4th elder-ancestor Riyao-gong (日燿公, wife Lady Zheng) with two sons Chengjin and Chengyu, and Chengjin-gong (wife Lady Zhang) with one son named Keren (刻仁).

pt1_32.en: Genealogical name register continuing a descent line (the surrounding pages run in the low-to-mid teens of 世/generations for the Jiang lineage). It records men such as Renyou (仁友), Yonglong (永隆), Yulong (裕隆), Yuanyou (淵友) and Tilong (提隆), each with wife's surname (Hong 洪, Lie 列, Li 李, Dong 董, Chen 陳, etc.) and their sons, including notes of an adopted heir (Yulong taking Yonglong's youngest son to continue the line). No firm dates given on this page.

pt1_33.en: Continuation of the same name register. Lists descendants such as Tian'en (天恩), Yuanlong (遠隆), and the fifth/sixth elder uncle-ancestors named Huan (煥), with wives (Zhu 朱, Yan 顏, Ye 葉) and sons. Notes that this branch resided at Shanzixia-Heshang (山子下河上) and a burial at Xinfa (新發). Several characters are marked [unclear] in the original (birth years and some month/day details illegible).

pt1_34.en: Name register continuing the line. Records men such as Chaoxu (啁煦/朝煦), Lilong (禮隆), and the eighth uncle-ancestor named Huang (晃), with wives (Liu 劉) and sons, including grandsons named Chaohu (朝鵠) and Chaohuang (朝晃) and their sons (the Jingzhou 荊州 / Qizhou 戚州 lines). Notes residence near Xinfa-xia / Shanzixia (新發下、山子下). Several birth years and dates are [unclear] in the original.

pt1_35.en: Name register continuing the Jingzhou/Qizhou and Chaohuang (朝晃) sub-branches. Lists sons of the Huaixiang (槐祥), Huaizong (槐宗), Huaiqing (槐清), Qizhou (戚州) and Chaohuang lines, with given names of grandsons (Weizhou 維州, Dingzhou 定州, etc.) and their sons (Qilong 起龍, Qifeng 起鳳, Qipeng 起朋). Notes the family resided at a place called Guiyutan (歸魚潭) in the Guiyan-Dayuan (歸言大園) area. One line (Huaiqing) noted as having no recorded heirs.

pt1_36.en: Register mixing names with grave/feng-shui notes. Mentions an ancestor styled Li (禮公) whose heirs are unrecorded, and burial details at Xinfa (新發) with geomantic orientations (e.g. xin-shan/yi-xiang 辛山乙向, and a 'snake-form' 蛇形 grave). Lists ancestral wives surnamed Guan (關) and Lei (雷) and notes a re-repair of a grave on the 19th of the 8th month. Also records the Chen-surname ancestors at Bengcheng (崩城) and brothers Chaodong (朝洞), Chaoyong (朝泳), Chaowei (朝渭). Much of the page is [unclear] in the original.

pt1_37.en: Register listing nine brothers of the Chao- (朝) generation: Chaojun (朝俊), Chaowo (朝渥), Chaodong (朝洞), Chaoyi (朝鎰), Chaozong (朝宗), Chaoyang (朝陽), etc. Focuses on the eldest great-uncle-ancestor Chaowei (朝渭) and his wife (surname Yao/Hu), with burial sites at Xinfa (新發) and geomantic orientations, and his three sons (Zhouwei 週渭, and two more), continuing into the next generation. Many birth years and personal names are [unclear] in the original.

pt1_38.en: Name register heavily damaged at the top (multiple [unclear] marks). Records a line producing three sons Xiankai (獻開), Xianming (獻明), Xianxiu (獻秀) — with a note that Xiankai died young — and a parallel line Liukai (劉開) producing Xianli (獻理), Xianwu (獻五), Xianlong (獻龍). Continues to the next generation with sons named ...chang (昌), e.g. Yuchang (宇昌), Qingchang (慶昌), Chengchang (成昌), Fuchang (福昌), each with wives' surnames. Opening lines are too damaged to read reliably.

pt1_39.en: Register of the Xian- (獻) and ...chang (昌) generations. Lists Xianlong (獻龍), Yunxiang (雲驤), Xianqiu (獻球), Xianqi (獻琪), Xianlin (獻琳) and their wives (Peng 彭, Yan 顏, Zhong 鍾, Li 李) and sons — many sons bearing the generational element 昌 (Xuechang 學昌, Shichang 時昌, Sichang 泗昌, Zhaochang 昭昌, etc.). One son noted as having died young [unclear].

pt1_40.en: Register of the Yun- (雲) and Xian- (獻) generations. Lists Lixing (禮興), Yunxiang (雲驤), Yunhui (雲輝), Yunbin (雲彬) and their wives (He 何, Yan 顏, Pan 潘) and sons, mostly named with the elements 獻 (Xianli 獻理, Xianqiong 獻琼, Xianyao 獻瑤, etc.) and 昌 (Lichang 麗昌, Nanchang 南昌, etc.). Notes one man with two wives (Yan 顏 and Gao 高) who together had four sons. Several names are [unclear].

pt1_41.en: Register headed '30th-generation ancestor Wei (三十世祖渭公)' tracing his descent line. Lists Wenwei (文渭), Kongwei (孔渭) and others with wives (Zhong 鍾, Liu 劉) and sons named with the elements 元 (Yuanjing 元荊, Yuanzhang 元章), 九 (Jiurun 九潤, Jiuhan 九漢, Jiuhong 九洪) and 奕 (Yizhang 奕章, Yiyun 奕運). Notes one heirless man (Yizhang 奕章) for whom an heir was brought in from the Shilin (世麟) line. Many birth dates and given names are [unclear].

pt1_42.en: Register continuing the Yun- (雲) / Xian- (獻) and ...han (漢) lines. Lists Yunhui (雲輝) with wife Li (李) and four sons (Xianrui 獻瑞, Xianrong 獻瑢, Xiandian 獻鈿, Xianchun 獻瑃), and the Honghan (宏漢), Ronghan (榮漢), Shanhan (善漢) brothers with wives (Zhang 張, Huang 黃, Liu 劉) and sons named with 元. Notes that the descendants of Zhouhan-gong (週漢公) lived at a place rendered [unclear] in 'Jiang-wu' (江屋). Some characters [unclear].

pt1_43.en: Short, partly blank register of the Shi- (世), Jiu- (九) and Yi- (奕) generations. Records Shirong (世榮, wife Zeng 曾), Jiuyue (九鑰), Jiuqing (九清, whose son was Yitu 奕圖), Yitu and his sons (Yiding 奕鼎, Yichang 奕昌), and Shibiao (世標, wife Zeng 曾). Several entries note 'had children' (生下) with no names filled in; some wives' surnames are left blank in the original.

pt1_44.en: Register of the Shi- (世) and Yi- (奕) generations. Records Shifu (世福), Shilu (世祿), Shilin (世麟), and Chengle (承樂) — the last noting that he and his wife (surname Huang 黃) died together on the 17th day of the 8th month of Xianfeng 9 (1859), the husband aged 79 and wife 67, leaving two sons (eldest Yilong 奕龍). Continues with Yilong's five sons (Shichuan 世傳, Shiye 世業, etc.) and their wives. Several names and entries are [unclear] or left blank.

pt1_45.en: Register of the Yi- (奕), Shi- (世), Jiu- (九) and Cheng- (承) generations. Records Yichang (奕昌, wife He 何) and his three sons Shigao (世高), Shikuan (世寬), Juqing (劇清), plus the Jiu- (九) line and Cheng- (承) line men (Chenggong 承恭, Chengkuan 承寬, etc.) with wives and sons. Many entries note 'had children' (生下) with names blank, and several given names are [unclear] in the original.

pt1_46.en: Register of the Cheng- (承), Ju-/Ji- (劇), Jiu- (九), Yuan- (元) and Yi- (奕) generations. Records Chenglie (承烈, wife Zeng 曾, son Juqi 劇祺), a Yuan- (元) ancestor (wife Zhang 張) with sons Jiuxu (九戌) and another, and continuing to Chengnan (承南, wife Chen 陳) whose sons Yifang (奕芳) and Yiqin (奕琴) lead to Shizhan (世展). Several given names are [unclear] and some entries left blank in the original.

pt2_01.en: A generational name register listing male ancestors with their wives (e.g. Shiyuan married a Liang 氏, Guisheng married a Dai 氏, Axing married a Liu 氏, etc.) and their sons. It records several 'Bo' (伯, elder-branch) ancestors with the generational name element 'Chao' (朝) — Chaomu, Chaocheng, Chaoyang, Chaocheng — noting how many sub-branches (房) each produced. No dates are given, and several entries are marked [unclear]; one line notes a descent line as 'not yet known' (其嗣未詳).

pt2_02.en: A register for the 'Jiu' (救) ancestors of the 'Chao' (朝) generation — Chaojian, Chaozong, Chaoyang — with their wives (Liu 氏, Wen 氏) and sons. It notes a son named Longqi (龍起) who was later brought in as heir to ancestor Chaocheng. A partly legible note states a man was born in a yi-si year of the Daoguang era (likely 1845) in Longzhou county (龍州縣), and that the family came to Xin'an (新安) beginning in the Kangxi period (1662–1722); details of moves back and forth and burial sites are largely [unclear]. The line closes with four sub-branches: Longqiu, Longtan, Longzhen, Longcai. Many entries are marked [unclear].

pt2_03.en: A register of men whose names begin with 'Gu' (古) — Guxiang, Guxing, Guqian, etc. — with their wives (mostly Liu 氏) and sons. Notable annotations: one man died young (早歲) without heirs, and one went to 'Gold Mountain' (金山, i.e. California / overseas) and died without heirs. The branch produces sons Gucai and Gufa. Several characters are [unclear].

pt2_04.en: A descent register beginning with Long-yan Gong (龍琰公) and tracing through Qirong, Shaofu, Chengwen and others, listing wives (Dai 氏, Mao 氏, Yan 氏, Chen 氏) and the sons of each, with several branches (房) noted. One entry records a second son who died young (亞二早歲). Several names are [unclear].

pt2_05.en: A near-duplicate of page 2: a register for the 'Jiu' (救) ancestors of the 'Chao' (朝) generation — Chaocheng, Chaojian, Chaozong, Chaoyang — with wives and sons, including the note that a son Longqi (龍起) was brought in as heir to Chaocheng. It again mentions origin in the Daoguang era at Longzhou county (龍州縣) and the family's arrival at Xin'an (新安) from the Kangxi period (1662–1722), closing with four sub-branches: Longqiu, Longtan, Longzhen, Longcai. Many entries [unclear].

pt2_06.en: A near-duplicate of page 1: a generational name register listing ancestors (Shiyuan, Guisheng, Axing, Ayuan, Chonglian, Ahsheng) with their wives (Liang, Dai, Liu, Mao, Chen 氏) and sons, plus the 'Bo' (伯) elder-branch 'Chao' (朝)-generation ancestors and the number of sub-branches each produced. No dates; several entries [unclear].

pt2_07.en: A descent register beginning with Long-qiu Gong (龍球公), tracing through Qirong, Shaofu, Chengwen and others, listing wives (Dai, Mao, Yan, Chen 氏) and sons, with four sub-branches (房) noted under Shaofu. One entry records a second son who died young. Nearly identical in structure to page 4; several names [unclear].

pt2_08.en: A register of 'Gu' (古)-generation men with their wives (mostly Liu 氏) and sons — closely parallel to page 3. Annotations note men who died young without heirs and at least two who went to 'Gold Mountain' (金山, California/overseas) and died without heirs; the branch yields sons Gucai and Gufa. Several characters [unclear].

pt2_09.en: This page is too faded to transcribe or translate reliably.

pt2_10.en: A descent register beginning with a Long-(龍) ancestor [unclear given name], tracing Qirong, Shaofu, Chengwen, Shaokuan and others, with wives (Dai, Mao, Yan, Chen, Liu 氏) and sons. Parallel to pages 4 and 7. Many names are partly illegible, including sons whose names survive only as Guo-(國) and Guofeng. Several entries [unclear].

pt2_11.en: A register of men in the 'Yong' (永) and 'Shao' (紹) generations — Qiqing, Yongchuan, Yonghu, Shaoli, Shaoxun, Shaoxin, Yongchan, Yongyou, Yongpeng, Yongcong — with their wives (Mao, Liu, Yan, Gu 氏) and sons. It covers a few generations of one branch; several wives' surnames and given names are [unclear].

pt2_12.en: A biographical/genealogical note centered on Long-cai Gong (龍彩公) and his line, mixing register entries with dated prose. It records three sub-branches and names Qixun (起燻) and Qitong (起通). For Qixun's line it gives a birth in the bing-zi year of the Qianlong era (likely 1756), in the eleventh month, 29th day, and a death in a year of the Jiaqing era (嘉慶, 1796–1820, exact year [unclear]), eighth month, with burial at age fifty-four. Wives' surnames and several dates and place details are [unclear]. The passage reads as a memorial to the founding (開基) ancestor of this branch, though much of it is illegible.

pt2_13.en: A fragmentary eulogistic prose passage praising an ancestor [Jin-ting Gong? 晉庭公, name unclear] as upright and selfless (公正無私), entrusted by clan consensus to hand down family matters, and saying the descendants owed much to this ancestor's virtue (多賴此公之德). It mentions burial in the family's own land (本園) near a watercourse/gully, a date of the eighth month, 25th day at the chen hour, and ends with register lines: his wife née Chen bore a son Shaoxian (紹現), who in turn (wife née Liu) had issue, with three sub-branches produced. The great majority of the text is marked [unclear].

pt2_14.en: A register noting 'three sub-branches produced' and then listing Yonghu, Yonghong and 'Gu' (古)-generation descendants — Gujun, Gujie, Guqiao — with their wives (Yan, Yang, Zhou, Chen, Liu, Zhang 氏) and sons such as Jinbao, Fulai, Mulai, Ayuan. Covers a few generations of one branch; several given names are [unclear].

pt2_15.en: A register of 'Shi' (士)-generation men and their forebears — Shiyong, Chenghao, Shixun, Shijun, Shichen, and the ancestors Shaoyan and Suodong — with wives (Lü, Liu, Zhong, Zhao, Wen 氏) and sons. One entry notes a burial at Qingshan (青山). Several names and the relationships are partly [unclear].

pt2_16.en: A register centered on Shaolin Gong (紹琳公, school-name Yaozong 耀宗, styled 'Kaizu' 開祖) and the 'Shi' (士)-generation men of his line — Shibo, Shixu, Shiwei, with sons/heirs Chengbo, Chengfa and others. Wives' surnames include Hong, Sun, Zhong, Liu, Ye and Chen 氏, with second marriages (續妻) noted; one man (Shixu) had no heir (無嗣). Several entries are [unclear].

pt2_17.en: A register of 'Shi' (士)-generation descendants — Shirong, Tianyou, Shimao, Shifen, Shiwei — with their wives (Ling, Ye, Chen, Wu, Zhang, Shen 氏) and sons such as Tianyou, Guowen, Guojun and Tianfu. It covers one branch over a couple of generations; several given names and one continuation line are [unclear].

pt2_18.en: A very short register fragment for the Fifth Branch (第五房). It names Chenglu (承祿), whose wife was a Madam Guo (郭氏), and a descendant Chengde (成德). Most details are [unclear] due to illegible marks.

pt2_19.en: A grave / biographical record for the 16th-generation ancestor Jiang Gong Chaoxing (江公朝興), style-name Chengxiang (成祥). He died and was buried; much of the dating is illegible, but a death in a 丁未 (dingwei) year, twelfth month, is mentioned, and the text says he lived to roughly age eighty [unclear]. It describes his burial site (a place rendered as Nibu / 坭塢圍) with notes on the mountain orientation (坐...向...) for geomantic purposes, and instructions that later descendants should follow regarding the grave. His wife, the ancestress Madam Chen (陳氏), is also recorded with a partial birth/death date (third month, tenth day) and a separate burial place. Several names, dates and place-names are marked illegible, so specifics are [unclear].

pt2_20.en: A register of two main branches descending from the 16th generation. It names Longyue Gong (龍躍公), a county-school licentiate (庠生) with the formal name Yunzhou (運洲), and Longjian Gong (龍見公), recorded as a 16th-generation ancestor born in a you (酉) year who lived to age 74. It then lists Longjian's three sons of the next generation — Qirun (起潤), Qizhou (起洲) and Qiyi (起溢) — and notes that Qiyi's line (via wives Madam Lin 林氏 and Madam Liu 劉氏) produced sons including Shaolin (紹琳), Shaoyan (紹彥) and Shaoqian (紹千). Some dates are [unclear].

pt2_21.en: A generational register listing the Shao (紹) and Lie (烈) generations with their wives and children. It covers Shaowan (紹萬) and his sons Lieying (烈英) and Liechang (烈場), then their offspring Daxian (大顯), Daxiang (大祥), Dale (大樂), Yafu (亞福), Yabing (亞炳) and others. Spouses' surnames (He 何, Liu 劉, Wen 溫, Hong 洪) are noted. A few names are [unclear].

pt2_22.en: A register of the Cheng (承) and Qi (起) generations. It notes several lines that ended without heirs (無嗣), including under Chenglu (承劉) and another Cheng-generation man. It records Qirun Gong (起潤公, wife Madam Gan 甘氏) and his son Shaoyi (紹溢), whose sons Chengzhen (承振) and Chengxin (承新) are listed — Chengzhen recorded as without heir. Several names are [unclear].

pt2_23.en: A short register/biographical fragment. It lists Sunxin (孫新) and sons Daxian (大顯), Chenbao (陳保) and Jinfu (進福), with some wives' names lost. It then notes Qirong Gong (起溶公), with a partial age (fourteen / 十四歲) [unclear], and records two branches: Shaolie (紹烈) and Shaofeng (紹鳳). Many entries are illegible, so details are [unclear].

pt2_24.en: A register of the Lie (烈) and Da (大) generations. It lists Shaolie (紹烈) and his sons Liexi (烈禧), Liechu (烈初) and others; Chengfu (承福) and sons Linqiao (林橋), Yashou (亞壽), Daheng (大恆); and notes an adoption — a sonless line that established Liezu (烈祖) as heir, whose sons were Dayou (大佑), Dakun (大昆), Guangxiu (光秀) and Yasi (亞四). Spouse surnames (Liu 劉, Zhao 趙) are noted. Some names are [unclear].

pt2_25.en: A register of the Shao (紹) / Cheng (承) / Da (大) generations, opening with a faded line about a man's descendants flourishing over many years and a place reference (珊鄰 / Shanlin?) [unclear]. It lists Shaoqing Gong (紹慶公), Chengrui (承瑞) and his sons Daming (大明), Dasheng (大生), Lizhen (利珍), plus Dali (大利), Chengwei (承威) and others. Spouse surnames (Liu 劉, Hong 洪, Zeng 曾, Liao 廖, Yang 楊) are noted. Several entries are [unclear].

pt2_26.en: A register of the Da (大) and Cheng (承) generations. It lists Dayou (大佑), Chengzhong (承種) and sons Daqing (大清), Dazhan (大展); Dazhan's children Yaren (亞仁) and others; and notes two adoptions, where Chengli (承禮) and Songsheng (松生, wife Madam Dai 戴氏) each took a son as heir (繼嗣). Also lists Liezhen (烈珍) with sons Yaxiang (亞祥) and Yafeng (亞鳳). A few names are [unclear].

pt2_27.en: A biographical / grave record for the 17th-generation ancestor Jiang Longyue Gong (江龍躍公), a county-school licentiate (庠生), formal name Yunzhou (運洲). He was born in a Kangxi-era dingyou (丁酉) year — within the Kangxi reign (1662–1722), so roughly 1717 [unclear] — on the 22nd day; many of the dating details and geomantic notes are illegible. The eulogy praises his character: a man who cultivated virtue, filial and friendly, diligent and frugal, accumulating merit for the family over nine generations [unclear]. He was buried near (or together with the plot of) Qirun Gong (起潤公), on auspicious ground said to bring prosperity. His wife, the ancestress Madam Liu (劉氏), is also recorded with a separate burial place. The record closes by noting he produced nine main branches (生下九大房). Specific dates are [unclear].

pt2_28.en: A register centered on the line of Dakun (大昆), opening with a note that his descendants were numerous (子孫繁...). It lists Dakun (wife Madam Chen 陳氏) and following Cheng (承) and Da (大) generation members, including Shaowen (紹溫), Chenggeng (承庚) and his sons Dayi (大義), Dayao (大耀) and Yasi (亞四). Many entries are heavily illegible, so the lineage detail is [unclear].

pt2_29.en: A register for the Third Branch (三房), headed by Qidu Gong (起渡公) / Qilian Gong (起濂公), listing a numbered set of Qi-generation (起) brothers — e.g. Qijun (起浚), Qiyan (起儼), Qijin (起溍), Qiwen (起文), Qiyuan (起淵). It then records Shaoying (紹瑩) and Shaorun (紹潤) with wives (Madam Yao-Zou 姚鄒氏, Madam Yao-Zheng 姚鄭氏) and their Cheng-generation (承) sons, down to a Da-generation child Dayao (大堯). Several characters are [unclear].

pt2_30.en: A register for the Third Branch (三房) under Qijun Gong (起俊公). It lists Shaorun Gong (紹潤公, wife Madam Shen 沈氏) and his sons Shaomu (紹沐), Shaohu (紹湖), Shaoshen (紹深); Shaoying (紹瑩, wife Madam Yao-Ruan 姚阮氏) and sons Chengcai (承財), Chengshen (承珅), Chengqi (承琦); and further Cheng- and Da-generation members (Chengzong 承宗, Chenghua 承華, Damen 大盟, Chengrong 承榮, Guifu 貴福). Some entries are [unclear].

pt2_31.en: A register continuing the Cheng (承) and Da (大) generations of the Third Branch. It lists Chengqi (承琦) and son Dachao (大潮); Yongqi (永琦), noted without heir (無嗣); Yongyuan (永遠); Chengrong (承榮); and a string of Da-generation men — Dachuan (大傳), Daxiang (大翔), Dazhou (大周), Dahuan (大煥) and others — plus Shaoshen Gong (紹深公). Many wives' surnames and given names are illegible, so details are [unclear].

pt2_32.en: A register for the Fourth Branch (四房) under Qijin Gong (起溍公). It lists Shaohu Gong (紹湖公) with wives Madam Zhang (張氏) and Madam Zheng (鄭氏) and sons including Fajin (發金), Chengcheng (承程), Chengyuan (承元), Chengfu (承福), Chengzhu (承柱); plus Shaoying (紹瑩), Shaojing (紹精), Shaoshen (紹深) lines, down to Chengcan (承燦) and his sons Datang (大堂), Dalian (大連), Yasi (亞四). A few names are [unclear].

pt2_33.en: A register for the Fifth Branch (五房) under Qiyuan Gong (起源公). It runs through Shao (紹), Yong (永), Da (大), Chang/Si (昌/司) and Hong (宏)/Dong (東) generations, listing numbered sub-lines such as the brothers Jige (吉閣), Jixiang (吉祥), Jirui (吉瑞), Jijin (吉近) and their sons (Hongyao 宏耀, Hongwen 宏文, Hongxiang 宏祥, Hongzhi 宏志, Hongzhong 宏忠, Hongqian 宏錢, and Dong-generation sons Dong'an 東安, Dongsheng 東勝, Dongyou 東友, Donghe 東和). Spouse surnames (Liu 劉, Chen 陳) are noted; several characters are [unclear].

pt2_34.en: A register of the Da (大), Cheng (承) and Chang (昌) generations (continuing the Fifth Branch). It lists Dadian (大殿) and sons Yangjiao (楊嬌), Yangfa (楊發), Yangsheng (楊勝); Chengjia (承甲) and sons Daxun (大勳), Daduan (大端); Huoxun (火勳) and sons Changhua (昌華), Changmao (昌茂); Dahu (大鵠) and sons Changrong (昌榮), Changyi (昌義); and Chengge (承閣) with sons Dajin (大進), Dali (大裡), Dagui (大貴). Spouse surnames (Liu 劉, Li 李, Lu 盧) are noted; a couple of entries are [unclear].

pt2_35.en: A generational name register continuing the descendants of Shaorun (紹潤) and his sons. It lists husbands, their wives (by surname), and the sons born to each — e.g. Dajin (大進), Dali (大理), Dagui (大貴), and the lines of Chengke (承科) and Chengxue (承學) down to grandsons such as Daozhong (道中), Daocheng (道成), and Daoxin (道信). No dates are given; several names are marked [unclear].

pt2_36.en: Heading 'Sixth house: Qiyou Gong (六房 起又公)'. A short name register for this sixth branch, listing fathers, wives by surname, and sons (e.g. Chengge 承閣 → Daqiu 大球; Damei 大美 → Huosheng 火生), ending with the wife née Yao (姚萬氏) who bore Shaoqi (紹淇), Shaodong (紹洞), and Shaohai (紹海). Many names are [unclear]; no dates.

pt2_37.en: A biographical sketch of Shaoqi Gong (紹淇公), whose school name was Yuansheng (淵生), styled 'Eryou-chuang' (二又創). The text praises his character and notes that he founded an enterprise [mention of 'nine rooms/buildings' 九間], but the page is very badly damaged — almost every phrase is marked [unclear], so the details of his life, dates, and deeds cannot be reconstructed reliably. It closes by recording his wife née Yao-Shen (姚沈氏), who lived to about eighty (壽八旬), and their sons, including Chengxiang (承祥) and others whose names are [unclear].

pt2_38.en: A name register continuing Shaoqi's descendants — fathers, wives by surname, and sons. It records lines such as Chunyu (純玉), Dalin (大林), and the Xu (旭) generation (Xuhui 旭輝, Xuzhao 旭昭, Xuqing 旭清), down to grandsons like Zhousheng (周生), Guangsheng (廣生), Jisheng (吉生), and Qingsheng (慶生). No dates; several names [unclear].

pt2_39.en: A name register for the line of Damo (大模, also given the name Cheng-... and the sobriquet 'Gudong' 古洞氏) and of Chenglu (承祿, named Mingzhu 明珠). It lists wives by surname and sons of the Xu (旭) generation — Xuqing (旭清), Xuyuan (旭源), Xuhao (旭浩) — and a group of sons including Dagang (大剛), Dapeng (大朋), Daliu (大柳), Dajian (大劍), and Dayong (大永). No dates.

pt2_40.en: A name register of the Xu (旭) generation, listing fathers, wives by surname (with several second wives / 續 noted), and sons whose given names mostly end in '-de' (德): Zude (祖德), Chunde (純德), Rende (仁德), Wude (武德), etc. Lines include Xuxiang (旭祥), Xuhuang (旭煌), Xudong (旭東), and Xugao (旭高). No dates; opening line and several names [unclear].

pt2_41.en: A name register for the line of Daliu (大柳), Dapeng (大朋), and their kin, listing wives by surname (several with second wives noted), and sons of the Xu (旭) generation — Xuxiang (旭祥), Xuhuang (旭煌), and others — plus grandsons such as Shishou (石壽) and Pingde (平德). No dates; several names [unclear].

pt2_42.en: A name register for the line of Dayong (大永), Dagang (大剛), and related branches, listing wives by surname and sons of the Xu (旭) generation (Xuxiang 旭祥, Xudi 旭帝, Xuxin 旭信, etc.) down to grandsons. A note mentions an adoptive/continuation arrangement [unclear]. No dates; several names [unclear].

pt2_43.en: A short name register for the Xu (旭) generation and the line of Chengdao (承道), listing wives by surname and sons such as Dalun (大倫), Dacai (大材), Dati (大梯), Dasui (大穗), and the next generation Xubo (旭波), Xushun (旭順), Musheng (木生). A note records an adoption of Dalun as heir to Guanzhang (官長) [unclear]. No dates.

pt2_44.en: A name register for the lines of Dati (大梯), Dasui (大穗), and Shaozhao (紹沼), listing wives by surname and sons of the Xu (旭) generation (Xurun 旭潤, Xushun 旭順) and the Da- generation (Dayuan 大元, Dali 大梨, Daluan 大鸞). No dates; several names [unclear].

pt2_45.en: A name register continuing the lines of Xuzhi (旭制), Daluan (大鸞), Chengqi (承祺), Daqin (大欽), and Chengtan (承談), listing wives by surname and sons such as Xuchu (旭初), Xurun (旭潤), Xuchao (旭潮), Xubiao (旭標), Dacheng (大誠), Daying (大英). No dates; several names [unclear].

pt2_46.en: A name register for the lines of Xubiao (旭標), Dacheng (大誠), Damao (大茂), Chengji (承紀), and Dayong (大雍), listing wives by surname and sons of the Xu (旭) generation (Xuao 旭瑙, etc.). One line notes a wife 'aged eight' [八歲 — likely a child-betrothal or transcription oddity, unclear]. No dates.

pt2_47.en: A name register for the lines of Daying (大英), Chengwu (承五, sobriquet Changsi 昌姒), and Dazhen (大鎮), listing wives by surname and sons of the Xu (旭) generation — Xupeng (旭朋), Xuxing (旭興), Xukai (旭開) — and earlier sons such as Yonglie (永列) and Jinyang (金楊). No dates; several names [unclear].

pt2_48.en: A short name register for the lines of Chengye (承頁), Dalai (大來), Chengrun (承潤), and Shaolian (紹漣), listing wives by surname and sons such as Dayuan (大苑), Dengsheng (灯生), Malan (瑪瀾), Chengfu (承富), Chengzhen (承貞), Dayu (大欲), and Daquan (大全). No dates.

pt2_49.en: A name register for the lines of Dacheng (大成), Dashe (大舍), Chengjian (承劍), Daqin (大欽), and Mahu (瑪瑚), listing wives by surname and children including Ayun (亞運), Ajia (亞嘉), Awang (亞旺), Ayuan (亞圓), and a note that Mahu's wife née Luo (羅氏) bore sons Wuren (戊仁), Diping (迪平), and daughters Zilan (紫蘭), Shuyi (淑義), 'and five more daughters'. One note records Daqin as a celibate/childless figure (童子) [unclear]. No dates.

pt2_50.en: A name register headed by Shaolan Gong (紹瀾公) and Shaochuan Gong (紹川公), covering the lines of Chengjian (承見), Chengzhi (承知), Chengyi (承奕), and Dagan (大乾), down to Yongkui (永魁) and Yongrong (永榮). Two figures (Chengyi and Chengyi's line) are noted as 'staff/officials' (職員) [unclear context]. No dates.

pt2_51.en: A short name register: the line of Daxu (大旭) and Shaoliu (紹流) with sons Chengchao (承超), Chenghan (承漢), Chengzhao (承招). The page ends with a heading introducing the 'Eighth house, rank ren' (八房行壬), Qiqing Gong (起清公), whose wife née Wen (文氏) bore Shaohao (紹顥), Shaojiang (紹江), Shaolao (紹勞), and Shaowang (紹汪). No dates.

pt2_52.en: A genealogical register listing descendants of Shaowang (紹汪) and his sons (Chengkui 承魁, Chengrun 承潤, Chengliang 承良 with their children) and, under the ninth branch (九房), Qiqian (起前) and wife Madam Zheng (鄭氏) with sons Shaoyang (紹洋), Shaoxiang (紹湘), Shaolan (紹蘭), Shaosi (紹汜). Lists wives' surnames and male offspring only; no dates given.

pt2_53.en: A name register for the line of Shaoyang (紹洋) and wife Madam Zeng (曾氏), covering his sons Chengti (承禔), Chengkui (承魁), Chengjiao (承教) and their children (e.g. Dahong 大鴻, Dadan 大旦). Wives' surnames are noted; no birth/death dates.

pt2_54.en: A short name register continuing the same branch: descendants of Chengjiao (承教), Dagu (大穀), and Shaoxiang (紹湘) with wife Madam Liu (劉氏) and sons Chengkai (承開), Chengti (承提). Lists wives and children only; no dates.

pt2_55.en: A name register covering Chengti (承提) and the line of Shaotan (紹潭) and wife Madam Xie (謝氏) with sons Chengti (承禔), Chengshi (承仕), Chengli (承利), Chengrun (承潤), plus a sub-list of children (Zhaoshou 照壽, Dashou 大壽, Datong 大同, Dalü 大律). No dates.

pt2_56.en: A name register listing descendants of Chengshi (承仕), Chengli (承利), Guanfu (官福), Chengrun (承潤, with a remarried wife Madam Zou 鄒氏), Dadian/Daxian (大獻), and Shaobao (紹包) with wife Madam Liu (劉氏). Wives and sons only; no dates.

pt2_57.en: A name register for Qiliang (啓亮), Dahao (大顥), and Chengjing (承敬) and their sons (Dayou 大有, Yasan 亞三, Dagui 大貴, Dagen 大根). Wives' surnames partly [unclear]; no dates given.

pt2_58.en: A section divider page containing only the heading "First Branch" (長房 / 'eldest house'). No names or dates.

pt2_59.en: A biographical/origin note for the ninth-generation ancestor Hong (洪公), also called Qilan (起瀾), a county academy student (庠名) named Dongqing (東淸). It praises him: in everyday life he read widely across many books [text partly unclear]. The dates are hard to read: it mentions a chou (丑) year and a wei (未) year, and gives his death in a year cyclically marked jiawu (甲午), on the first day of the tenth month [exact Western year unclear]. He was buried at a place called Dakeng Garden (大坑園) [remainder unclear, with a later reburial/move of the coffin noted]. His wife was Madam Wei (渭氏), with a later (continued) wife Madam He (何氏). He produced five great branches: the lines of Tonghan (通漢公), Tuan-something (團淲公) [name unclear], Shaohuai (紹淮公), Shaosi (紹泗公), and Shaoyan (紹炎公).

pt2_60.en: A generational register for the senior (eldest-uncle) line of Tonghan (通漢公) and wife Madam Liu (劉氏): son Chengtong (承統公), then Dachang (大昌公), then Yonglu (永祿) and brothers Dami (大覓公) and Daqi (大祺公). It marks the 10th and 20th generations (十世 / 廿世) and notes Yonglu's register-name Qinghui (清輝), his wife Madam Zhang (張氏) and a concubine Madam Liu (劉氏), with son Jigong (集恭) and others (集泰, 集淲). Spans roughly the 10th to 20th generations; no firm dates.

pt2_61.en: A name register for the lines of Dami (大覓公, wife Madam Liao 廖氏, son Yongfa 永發) and Daqi (大祺公) with sons Yongfa (永發), Yongji (永吉), Yonghe (永合), Yonghui (永輝); Yongji's wife Madam Zeng (曾氏) bore Jizhen (集珍). Notes seniority labels (伯/叔, elder/younger uncle). No dates.

pt2_62.en: A 19th-generation register: the second-uncle ancestor Tonghong (通洪公) and wife Madam Liang (梁氏), who took Shaohuai's second son Yongqiu (永球公) as heir (継嗣, adopted successor). Continues with Dagen (大根), Yongqiu, Da'an (大安公, wife Madam Lin 林氏) and sons Da'an/Dachang/Yongqing (大安, 大常, 永淸). One date fragment: Yongqing's wife Madam Liu is recorded as dying in the 12th year of the Guangxu era (光緒十二年 ≈ 1886) [month unclear].

pt2_63.en: A 19th-generation register: the third-uncle ancestor Shaohuai (紹淮公) and wife Madam Zeng (曾氏), with sons Yongfeng (永鳳) and Yonghuang (永凰); also Dachang (大常公, wife Madam Huang 黃氏). Includes the line of Chengji (承基公) with Chengji, Chengqiu (承球), Chengxun (承訓). Names and seniority labels only; no dates.

pt2_64.en: A 19th-generation register: the fifth-uncle ancestor Shaosi (紹泗公) and wife Madam Liu (劉氏), son Chengguo (承國); plus Chengxun (承訓公) with sons Dawen (大文), Jinfu (金福), Jinqi (金祈), and Chengguo with son Dake (大可). Wives' surnames noted; no dates.

pt2_65.en: A register naming a sixth-generation ancestor Jiang Mian-si (江綿泗公) and his sons Yongji (永繼公), Shaomian (紹綿公), Chengye (承業公); also Dake (大可公, wife Madam Zhang 張氏) and Yongfeng (永鳳). A repeated note about ancestor Shaomian (紹綿祖) being somewhere [unclear] is partly illegible. No firm dates.

pt2_66.en: A 20th-generation passage that records this branch's migration to Sabah. It lists ancestors Chengji (承繼公) and Chengye (承業公), and the 20th-generation ancestors Shaomian (紹綿公) and Chengye (承業公). It states that (his) wife Madam Liang (梁氏) went to Papar (巴邑, i.e. 吧巴 Papar) [and to a place rendered 那蘇義, likely 'Nasugi/Lansugi' locality near Papar — unclear], with the Christian/ritual name (禮名) Wangfu (望福). One son is named Dakai (大開). Wangfu's birth and death dates are largely illegible; a jiazi (甲子) year is mentioned for a birth and an age of sixty-three (六十三) at death, with the death late in some year [exact Western years unclear].

pt2_67.en: A 20th-generation biographical passage about the Sabah branch. The ancestor (承...公) had sons Dazhong (大忠公) and Daxin (大信公). Dazhong died young and was buried at a place [name partly unclear, '五有...仔']. Daxin (大信公) went to Papar (巴邑 / 吧巴), to the locality of 那蘇義 [unclear], and diligently built charcoal kilns (炭窰). He is described as gentle, generous, and hard-working — farming for a living, thrifty in running the household, accumulating a modest surplus. A date fragment mentions the early years of '隆城' [a place name, possibly Jesselton/Sandakan settlement — unclear] when he was about thirty (三十). His wife Madam Zhang (張氏) also went to 那蘇義, ritual name Wang-something (望...). Their children: a daughter named Yazhao (亞招) and sons Yongxin (永信), Yongzong (永宗), Changzu (昌祖) [some text unclear, including a wife/marriage to a 紹琴].

pt2_68.en: A 20th-generation passage (second of this group) with register-names recorded as Fugui (富瑰) and Yiyuan (毅淵), and a man Yongjia (永家). Birth and death dates are mostly illegible (a 25th-day death noted). His wife Madam Lai (賴氏) had the ritual name En-zhao (恩照). They had one son and a daughter [number/details unclear]. A large block at the end is hard to read but clearly concerns the Sabah settlement: it repeatedly names Beluran (剝利, i.e. the Beluran district) — a 'Beluran village' (剝利村), the 'Beluran church cemetery' (剝利教會陰地), a lime-mortar grave (石灰坟), and a stone marker/inscription (石碑記) [much of this section is unclear].

pt2_69.en: A birth/death register, mostly for the 23rd generation (二十三世). It lists men such as Junfeng (俊鳳), Jun'en (俊恩) and others with their birth dates given in Qing reign-era years — e.g. the Tongzhi (同治) and Guangxu (光緒) periods, roughly the 1870s–1890s — together with wives (e.g. a Lady Wang 王氏). One entry mentions a stele being erected to mark a grave [unclear], and several places of birth are noted but illegible (e.g. born at "...仔社" [unclear]).

pt2_70.en: A birth register for the 22nd–23rd generations (二十二世/二十三世). It records men including Junming (俊明), Daikai (大開), Anhu (安鵠), Wuyuan (屋員) and Jungong (俊恭), with birth dates in the Guangxu era (光緒, roughly 1876–1890). Notably several are recorded as born in Boli (剝利) — i.e. the Sabah emigrant branch — with notes on planting/cultivation [unclear].

pt2_71.en: A register entry for the 22nd–23rd generations centered on Yongren (永仁), ritual name Tongxing (同興), style Yan (燕), with wife Lady Guan (關氏). It gives his birth in a Tongzhi xinwei year, 11th month (roughly 1871) and death in the Guangxu gengyin year (1890), notes the burial is "not recorded in detail" [unclear], and lists children including a daughter Qiongdian (瓊典) and a son Guifeng (癸鳳).

pt2_72.en: A register of the 23rd generation, listing sons by birth-order (3rd Yaoci 耀慈, 2nd Yaoxiang 耀祥, 4th, 7th Yaoying 耀英) with Guangxu-era birth dates (1870s–1880s, several years left blank/illegible). Notable: Yaoying (耀英) is recorded as adopted out to / made heir of Yongzong (過繼永宗). Several names are unclear.

pt2_73.en: A register of the 23rd generation continuing the same family, listing children by birth-order (7th–10th): daughter Fuying (福英), son Yao'an (耀安), daughter Chenying (辰英) and son Yaozhen (耀珍), with births in the Guangxu era (己丑 ~1889, 亥 year ~1887, etc.). All are noted as "born to Yaojiu (耀九)" [or born in the Yaojiu line — unclear].

pt2_74.en: A register entry (22nd–23rd generations) for Yongzong (永宗), ritual name Tongfa (同發), born in the Guangxu renwu year, 9th month (1882). His wife is a Lady Zhou/Zhao [surname unclear, written 洲氏], and the entry records that Yaohua (耀華) was taken in as his (adopted) son.

pt2_75.en: A short memorial/biographical notice with a couplet, for the 22nd-generation ancestor Yonghong (永宏), ritual name Changfu (昌富), style Yijian (毅漸). He was born in a yisi year and died on the 23rd of a month [year unclear]. The eulogistic verse runs roughly: "It is heard that the Way of Heaven flows on, the five vital airs intermingling... for twenty years he upheld the household... may this be set down in a single stroke, that the lineage rise and endure for a thousand autumns" [several phrases unclear]. His wife was Lady Li (黎氏), ritual name Danzhao (旦照), who bore four sons and four daughters. The four sons are named: Junbian (俊邊), Junhua (俊華), Junming (俊明) and Junsen (俊森).

pt2_76.en: A register entry (22nd generation) for Jiru (集如), ritual name Junbian (俊邊), born in a guiyou year, 1st month. His wife is Lady Huang (黃氏). The entry notes a maternal-ancestor place "Lizhou Liusunkeng" (黎洲六孫坑) and lists at least one son, Daozhen (道珍), with a Guangxu 29 (~1903) date [several details unclear].

pt2_77.en: A register entry (22nd generation) for Jiru (集如), ritual name Junming (俊明), with wife Lady Chen (陳氏); dates are largely illegible. It lists his children (sons and daughters whose given names end in -zhen 珍, -chang 昌, -fang 方), but most names and dates are obscured [unclear].

pt2_78.en: A register of the 24th generation (二十四世) for Youqiao (有喬), milk-name Qichang (其昌), and his sons. It records the 6th son Qiqing (其清), born in the Xuantong 1 / 1909 jiyou year (the page gives the Western year explicitly as 1909), and the 7th son Qiyong (其永) born in the 8th year of the Republic (1919), with wife Lady Xu (徐氏). It also lists grandsons Hanqiang (漢強), Hansheng (漢昇) and Hanying (漢英) born in the early Republican period.

pt2_79.en: A short, largely faded register entry of the 24th generation for Youli (有利), milk-name unclear, listing a son Meijiu (美九) and a daughter Runzhen (閏珍); birth dates are illegible [unclear].

pt2_80.en: Opening of a prose essay titled "Regulations of the Ancestral Trust (嘗規)," composed by a later descendant, Shaoqing (紹慶公). It begins with a moral preamble: "Since ancient times no bond is closer than that of father and son, and no duty is greater than filial piety. To make one's name known and bring honor to one's parents — this is what the ancestors deeply hope for from their descendants..." It then turns to lineage history, recalling the great-granduncle ancestor Chaodong (朝洞公), who in an early reign-year set out from Hui prefecture (惠府) [Huizhou] to open new ground; the ancestor Chaoji (朝緝公) who reached the new settlement (新邑, i.e. Xin'an) and established the family's livelihood; and Chaozan (朝瓚公) and his wife who likewise migrated to Shouchao (守朝) and contributed to the founding effort. Many phrases are damaged [unclear].

pt2_81.en: Continuation of the Ancestral Trust essay, recounting how the trust fund was built up. It tells that earlier generations worked frugally and the family had no common estate; then in the 51st year of Qianlong (1786) one Dingwen (丁文公) [name partly unclear], finding there were no funds for the ancestral sacrifices, publicly took the lead in starting a fund. Contributions were levied per head — each was to put in fifty cash (錢五十文), accumulating toward roughly one thousand [cash] — and the principal grew with its interest ("mother and child," 子母). A signed agreement was drawn up and entrusted in turn to the elders/uncles for safekeeping and record. Over some twenty years a surplus accumulated; the fund was managed in succession, and around the Jiaqing 19th year (1814) Qisong (起溺公/起溺) took over the management for fourteen years, up to the 25th year, after which the accounts passed on again [many details unclear].

pt2_82.en: Continuation of the Ancestral Trust essay. It records that by the 26th year of Daoguang (1846) a descendant, Jiang Puying (蔣溥英) [name uncertain], and others continued to manage the accumulated fund, the spent and saved capital by then amounting to several thousand and more, so that the regular spring and autumn sacrifices were never lacking. It attributes this to the virtue of the ancestors and to the efforts of Wengong (文公), Tonggong (通公) and Nigong (溺公), exhorting later descendants to "carry on well and continue well" (善繼善述) what was begun. It reflects that in earlier years, when the clan members were few, only a dozen or so people handled the seasonal sacrifices, whereas later some thirty-odd people managed them — a passage celebrating the growth and unity of the lineage [several phrases unclear].

pt2_83.en: Continuation of the Ancestral Trust essay — a hortatory passage. It urges that even the young and able-bodied not grumble or be grudging over food and stipend, asking how, otherwise, one could follow the example of forebears and fulfill the sincerity of "honoring those who came before" (追遠). It calls on the uncles and clansmen to attend faithfully to the spring and autumn sacrifices to the ancestors and their wives (祖妣), each diligent in his duty and not treating the matter lightly. It promises that if these regulations are followed, the offerings will be ample, kinship will be renewed, and harmony preserved — so that the lineage and its blessings may continue unbroken for a thousand generations. Much of the text is damaged and several phrases are illegible [unclear].

pt2_84.en: The closing of the Ancestral Trust essay. It exhorts the uncles, nephews and clansmen who share in the trust's bounty to honor it together — to remember the hardship with which the successive ancestors built it up and the great toil with which the elders accumulated the fund — and to receive and pass it on to later generations; let this serve as the guiding preface (引). It cites a common saying that managing affairs and providing the sacrificial food takes effort, and hopes the uncles and nephews will act accordingly. It is signed and dated: a wuyin year [reign-name unclear; the text also reads "5th year, yimao"], in the last month of winter on an auspicious day, composed by the descendant Shaoqing (紹慶公) — the "Regulations of the Ancestral Trust (簽規)." The exact Western year is uncertain [unclear].
